items.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995
items.q: I toured with Count Basie, George Shearing, Billy Eckstine as a unit.

ctx.x: And tell us about the sound of that band, and how that worked in with the rhythm & blues kind of sound that you brought in your voice.

Well I think when everybody — I worked with Basie, of course. I toured with Count Basie, George Shearing, Billy Eckstine as a unit. I think that the Basie band was probably, of course it ended up being probably the most respected along with the Ellington, and Jimmy Lunceford orchestra. In those days we had dance bands, you see? In Raleigh-Durham, North Carolina they had what was called the “June German.” I don’t know if you’re familiar with that but if you ever do research on it, it was five days of dancing. It…
Well you know other artists have come in here and we’ve talked about the Basie band and they’ve said those exact words.

items.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995
items.q: I went into the studios with the likes of your Arnett Cobbs and your Count Basies and your Billy Eckstines, and I got to be on tour with these great people.

ctx.x: But he had a good ear though.

A great ear. And I think that that’s — Dizzy Gillespie told me that once when I got a chance to go to Japan the very first time. I went to Japan with Dizzy Gillespie and the Modern Jazz Quartet, and Sonny Stitt. And I was just so apprehensive because we were going to play the Budokan, and here I was this rhythm & blues artist, you know. And Dizzy said, “If you can hear it, you can sing it.” And I could always hear it. I don’t read © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

either, don’t read a note, you know, but always there are a lot of pictures of me looking at the music. It looks good. It gives me status, you know. Especially when I went to go into the studios with the likes of your Arnett Cobbs and your Count Basies and your Billy Eckstines, and I got to be on tour with these great people.
